title: Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025
official_title: To establish a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce, and to secure American leadership in deploying emerging technologies, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on April 29, 2025 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 62) after House action. Sponsored by a Republican member with four cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
summary: Establishes a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce administered by the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis. Section 2 adds eight responsibilities for the Assistant Secretary: promoting the stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the new Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks; encouraging reduced reliance of domestic manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of critical-good manufacturing to the United States and allies/partners. Section 3 requires the Assistant Secretary to establish, not later than 120 days after enactment, a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis (including the Departments of State, Defense, Homeland Security, Transportation, Energy, Agriculture, the Interior, and Health and Human Services; the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and the Small Business Administration). Within 1 year of enactment, the Assistant Secretary must carry out enumerated assessment, mapping, modeling, gap-identification, workforce, and coordination activities in consultation with the Working Group. The Assistant Secretary must designate — within 120 days of enactment, with public comment — critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods, updating those designations at least every 4 years. An implementation report is due to the relevant committees within 1 year after enactment. A national strategy and review of critical supply chain resiliency and manufacturing is due to the relevant committees within 18 months after enactment and annually thereafter — covering critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-critical supplies and services, substitutes, authentication/traceability methods (including blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies), and allies/key international partner nations; assessing the manufacturing base, supply chains, and workforce; identifying threats and supply chain shocks (with threats originating from section 7(2)(B) countries listed); and developing a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains. Reports may not include non-aggregated critical supply chain information, confidential business information, or classified information; a public comment period is required; reports are unclassified with an optional classified annex. Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (accompanied by a specified express statement) is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), is not subject to ex parte communication rules, may not be used against the submitter in civil actions or by other authorities without written consent, may not be disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act (with narrow exceptions), and does not constitute a waiver of trade-secret or other protections. The subsection does not apply to voluntary submissions in an application for federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry NDAA for FY2021 (Public Law 116-283). Section 4 requires the Secretary to submit, within 2 years of enactment, a Department of Commerce capability assessment identifying the duties, responsibilities, resources, programs, and expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, plus recommendations to enhance those activities and a strategy to implement them as appropriate. Section 5 provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title. Section 6 provides that the title and all its requirements terminate 10 years after the date of enactment. Section 7 defines all key terms — including "ally or key international partner nation" (which excludes countries posing a significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564), "critical good," "critical industry," "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c), "critical supply chain," "critical supply chain information," "domestic enterprise," "domestic manufacturer," "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act (title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276) and a named list including artificial intelligence, automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems, blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies, quantum computing and sensing, additive manufacturing, advanced manufacturing and IoT, nanotechnology, robotics, microelectronics and advanced computer hardware/software, semiconductors, and advanced materials science), "institution of higher education" (via 20 U.S.C. 1001), "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing), "manufacturing technology," "production equipment," "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce), "resilient critical supply chain," "Secretary" (of Commerce), "State," and "supply chain shock."
brief: Adds eight critical-supply-chain responsibilities to the Commerce Assistant Secretary for Industry and Analysis, establishes a 10-agency Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and a 120-day designation of critical industries/supply chains/goods, requires an implementation report (1 year), a national strategy and review (18 months + annual), a Department capability assessment (2 years), protects voluntarily-submitted supply chain information from FOIA/discovery, authorizes no additional funds, and sunsets the title 10 years after enactment.

items.main: Names the title the "Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Additional Responsibilities of Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis

items.main: Adds eight new responsibilities on top of the Assistant Secretary's existing duties: promoting stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting covered nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks (including by improving flexible manufacturing capacities and capabilities); encouraging reduced reliance of domestic enterprises and manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of manufacturing facilities that manufacture critical goods from section 7(2)(B) countries to the United States and allies/partners.
items.detail: Section 2 enumerates the eight paragraphs of added responsibilities.

sections.label: Section 3 — Critical Supply Chain Resilience Working Group

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must establish a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis, including the Department of State, the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the Small Business Administration.

Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, must assess, map, and model critical supply chains (including for critical and emerging technologies); identify high-priority gaps and vulnerabilities; identify potential supply chain shocks; evaluate the capability and capacity of domestic and allied manufacturers to serve as sources for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology; evaluate market-stability effects of disruption, strain, or elimination of a critical supply chain; evaluate the state of the manufacturing workforce (including identifying opportunities to create high-quality manufacturing jobs); and identify tools — including commercially available risk assessment tools — that leverage data and industry expertise to provide insights into critical supply chain vulnerabilities.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(1) — assessment activities in consultation with the Working Group.

items.main: In consultation with State and local governments, the Working Group, and (as appropriate) allies/key international partner nations: identify opportunities to reduce gaps and vulnerabilities; encourage consultation between the Federal Government, industry, nongovernmental representatives, higher education, and State/local governments; encourage consultation between the Federal Government and governments of allies/partners; identify opportunities to build U.S. capacity in critical supply chains, critical industries, and emerging technologies; identify opportunities to build allies/partners' capacity in critical industries and critical supply chains; and develop and assess contingency plans and coordination mechanisms.

Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must designate critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods; provide for a period of public comment and review; and update the designations not less than once every 4 years, including designations for technologies not described in section 7(12)(B) that the Assistant Secretary considers necessary.
items.detail: Subsection (d) — designations, public comment, and 4-year update cycle.

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must submit to the relevant committees of Congress an implementation report detailing supply chain activities conducted, describing supply chain data collected/retained/analyzed, identifying necessary tools including commercially available risk assessment tools, identifying all Federal agencies with authorities/responsibilities described in subsection (b), and identifying Federal agencies/programs/bureaus with duplicative purposes.

Not later than 18 months after enactment, and annually thereafter, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, covered nongovernmental representatives, industries, higher education, and State/local governments, must submit to the relevant committees a national strategy and review that identifies critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, designated critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-preparedness supplies and services, substitutes for critical goods/production equipment/manufacturing technology, methods and technologies for authentication and traceability of critical goods (including blockchain technology, distributed ledger technology, and other critical and emerging technologies as appropriate), and allies/partners; describes the U.S. manufacturing base, critical supply chains, and emerging technologies (including for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology) and the U.S. ability to maintain readiness and surge production; assesses and describes demand/supply, production by domestic manufacturers, and rural/Tribal/underserved-community effects; identifies threats and supply chain shocks — listing any threat or shock that may originate from a country (or entity/individual from a country) described in section 7(2)(B); assesses U.S. and allied manufacturing base resilience and workforce capacity; assesses flexible manufacturing capacity; and develops a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains.
items.detail: Subsection (f)(1) — 18-month national strategy and review with annual updates.

items.main: The national strategy report may not include critical supply chain information that is not aggregated, confidential business information of a private-sector entity, or classified information; the report is submitted in unclassified form and may include a classified annex; a public comment period is required.

Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must enter into an agreement with the head of any relevant agency to obtain any information, data, or assistance necessary to conduct subsection (b) activities.
Rule of construction: nothing in the section requires any private entity to share information with the Secretary or Assistant Secretary, to request assistance, or to implement any recommendation.

Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (identity of submitter included) — when accompanied by the specified express written or oral statement — is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3); is not subject to ex parte communication rules; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used directly by Commerce or any Federal, State, or local authority or third party in any civil action arising under Federal or State law when submitted in good faith; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used or disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act's purposes (with narrow exceptions for criminal investigation/prosecution and specified congressional/GAO oversight); may not, if provided to State or local governments, be made available under State/local disclosure law, distributed without consent, or used for purposes other than this section (or criminal investigation/prosecution); and does not constitute a waiver of any applicable privilege or protection under law, such as trade-secret protection.
items.detail: Subsection (i)(1)(A) — six enumerated protections tied to the express-statement mechanism in (i)(1)(B).

items.main: The voluntary submission mechanism does not apply to voluntary submissions of critical supply chain information in an application for Federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (Public Law 116-283).
items.detail: Subsection (i)(5) — semiconductor incentive program (FY2021 NDAA sec. 9902) application carveout.

sections.label: Section 4 — Department of Commerce Capability Assessment

items.main: Not later than 2 years after enactment, the Secretary must submit to the relevant committees a report — identifying duties/responsibilities/resources/programs/expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, assessing the purpose/legal authority/effectiveness/efficiency/limitations of each identified office or bureau, and providing recommendations to enhance activities (including improving effectiveness and coordination, and consulting with agencies implementing similar activities) — along with a strategy to implement the recommendations as appropriate.
No additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title.
This title and all requirements, responsibilities, and obligations under this title terminate 10 years after the date of enactment.

Defines key terms used in the title, including: "agency" (5 U.S.C. 551); "ally or key international partner nation" (excludes countries posing significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564); "Assistant Secretary" (Assistant Secretary of Commerce directing Industry and Analysis); "critical good"; "critical industry"; "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c); "critical supply chain"; "critical supply chain information"; "domestic enterprise"; "domestic manufacturer"; "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act, title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276, and a named list — artificial intelligence; automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems; blockchain and other distributed ledger, data storage, data management, and cybersecurity technologies; quantum computing and quantum sensing; additive manufacturing; advanced manufacturing and the Internet of Things; nanotechnology; robotics; microelectronics, optical fiber ray, and high performance and advanced computer hardware and software; semiconductors; advanced materials science); "institution of higher education" (20 U.S.C. 1001); "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing); "manufacturing technology"; "production equipment"; "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce); "resilient critical supply chain"; "Secretary" (of Commerce); "State" (each State, D.C., commonwealth, territory, possession, and each federally recognized Indian Tribe); and "supply chain shock" (an event causing severe or serious disruption, including a natural disaster, pandemic, biological threat, cyber attack, geopolitical conflict, terrorist or geopolitical attack, trade disruption caused by section 7(2)(B) countries or their entities/individuals, and Presidentially declared major disasters or emergencies under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170; 42 U.S.C. 5191)).

gaps: Section 7(2)(B) refers to "a country that poses a significant risk to the national security or economic security of the United States" — no list of such countries is provided within this title, leaving that determination to other law or executive designation.

The bill authorizes no additional funds (Section 5) but imposes new assessment, mapping, modeling, working-group, designation, reporting, and consultation obligations on Commerce and 10 other agencies.

The bill does not create any enforcement mechanism for the private-sector no-mandate rule of construction (Section 3(h)) or provide any incentive to submit voluntary information beyond the Section 3(i) protections.
The bill does not describe how the Assistant Secretary's four-yearly redesignations under Section 3(d) interact with the annual national strategy updates under Section 3(f).

featured_quotes.name: Mr. James
featured_quotes.text: I especially thank my chairman, friend, and mentor, the gentleman from Florida (Mr. Bilirakis), for his leadership and support. The gentlewoman has been a family friend for such a long time. I also have the pleasure of sharing the opportunity on this bill with Erin Houchin, my classmate; Robin Kelly; and Pat Ryan, my West Point classmate. This is an example of Congress coming together, reaching across the aisle, and working in the best interests of the American people.

added: Eight new statutory responsibilities on the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis (Section 2)
New Supply Chain Resilience Working Group of 10 named agencies, established within 120 days (Section 3)
120-day designation of critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods, with public comment and 4-year updates (Section 3(d))
18-month national strategy and review with annual updates and optional classified annex (Section 3(f))
2-year Department of Commerce capability assessment report (Section 4)
Voluntary-submission protections for critical supply chain information — FOIA exemption via 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), civil-action non-use, and disclosure restrictions (Section 3(i))
